opus-5.5.text:
I think one useful way to look at it is along two axes. The first is how hard the task is, roughly how much reasoning or exploration it needs. The second is how much the cost of getting it wrong matters, or how tolerant the setting is of errors.

At the easiest end are tasks where the agent does something a person could do quickly but finds tedious: filling forms, searching, summarizing, simple customer service flows. The value here is mostly saving time, and the bar for success is consistency more than brilliance.

The next tier is tasks that need real multi-step reasoning and interaction with an environment: writing and debugging code, doing research across many sources, operating software through a computer interface. These take a human hours rather than minutes. What matters here is long-horizon reliability, meaning whether the agent can keep track of context, recover from mistakes, and know when it's done. A lot of current progress is happening at this level. Coding is the clearest example, partly because the environment gives clear feedback: tests pass or they don't.

Then there's a frontier tier: tasks where even experts don't know the answer in advance, like scientific discovery, building a company, or making novel engineering decisions. These need creativity and the ability to define the problem, not just solve it. We're still early there.

The error-tolerance axis cuts across all of this. Some easy tasks are actually hard to deploy, because one mistake is very costly. Think of moving money or medical decisions. Some hard tasks are easier to deploy, because you can try many times and verify, like generating code with tests or proposing research ideas a human then filters. So the near-term sweet spot is often tasks that are hard enough to be valuable but where results can be verified cheaply. I think that's a big reason coding agents took off first.

The deeper point for me is that difficulty isn't only about intelligence. It's also about the environment, the feedback signals, and how well the task is specified. A lot of what makes agents work in practice is designing the right environment and evaluation, not just making the model smarter.

r001.rationale: The response classifies applications along two axes: task difficulty and the cost of errors, presenting them as distinct dimensions.

r002.rationale: It compares task demands to what humans can do, but does not say that human task difficulty may differ from difficulty for AI agents.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually think about it along two axes, and I find the second one matters more than people expect.

The first axis is the obvious one: how long is the task, and how much does it fuzz. Very short tasks, like "answer this factual question," are basically single-step. Medium tasks are things like "write a function that passes these tests" or "find the cheapest flight meeting these constraints," which take maybe tens of steps and have a clear verifier. Long tasks are things like "resolve this GitHub issue in a repo you've never seen" or "run this research project for a week." The longer the horizon, the more errors compound, and the more the agent has to recover from its own mistakes rather than just avoid making them. That's roughly the SWE-bench to tau-bench to "do my job for a month" spectrum.

But the second axis, which I think is underrated, is: how much does the environment push back, and how clear is the feedback. Coding is actually a relatively friendly domain even though it looks hard, because you get a compiler, you get tests, you get a stack trace. The world tells you when you're wrong. Compare that to something like customer service in tau-bench, where the "environment" includes a human who may be confused, may lie, may change their mind halfway through. Or a web task where the page just silently didn't do what you expected. The feedback is sparse and noisy, so the difficulty isn't really the reasoning, it's figuring out what state you're even in.

So if you put those together, you get a kind of grid. Short horizon plus dense feedback is basically solved. Long horizon plus dense feedback is where a lot of the current progress is, which is why coding agents are moving so fast. Long horizon plus sparse, ambiguous feedback is the hard quadrant, and that's where most real-world work actually lives.

One more thing I'd add is that difficulty for an agent is not the same as difficulty for a human. We tend to classify tasks by how hard they feel to us, but models find some "hard" things trivial and some "easy" things, like reliably clicking the right button on a messy web page, surprisingly brutal. So whenever I classify agent tasks, I try to ask: where does the error actually come from? Is it a reasoning gap, a knowledge gap, or a grounding gap, meaning the model just can't tell what happened? Those need totally different fixes, and lumping them under one "difficulty" score hides that.

r001.rationale: The response describes task difficulty along two axes—task horizon and environmental feedback—and combines them in a grid.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says difficulty for an agent is not the same as difficulty for a human, and that tasks humans find hard may be trivial for models and vice versa.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to classify agent applications is by how clearly the task is defined and how easily you can verify success. The number of steps matters, but it isn’t the whole story. A task can involve many steps and still be relatively easy if each step has clear feedback.

At one end, you have tasks where both the goal and the procedure are clear: retrieve some information, fill out a form, or execute a predefined workflow. The agent mainly needs to carry out instructions reliably.

Then you have tasks where the goal is clear, but the path isn’t. Coding is a good example. You know what behavior you want, and you may have tests, but the agent has to explore the codebase, try a solution, observe failures, and revise it. Here, the ability to interact with an environment becomes much more important.

At the harder end, even the goal or the evaluation criteria may be ambiguous. If you ask an agent to do research or improve a product, it has to help determine what is worth doing and what counts as a good result. That requires more judgment and more interaction with people.

So I would look at how much uncertainty the agent has to resolve, and what feedback is available to resolve it. That also helps explain where autonomy is practical: when success is easy to check, you can give the agent more room to try things. When success is difficult to judge, human involvement becomes much more important.

r001.rationale: The candidate classifies tasks by goal clarity, procedure clarity, uncertainty, and feedback, but does not state or imply that these dimensions of difficulty are orthogonal.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses agent task difficulty, but does not compare it with human task difficulty or say that the two may differ.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to classify agent applications is by how well-defined the task is, how long it takes, and how easy it is to verify success. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

At the simpler end, you have a task with a clear goal and a short path: find some information, call a tool, return an answer. Then you have tasks that require multiple steps, like fixing a bug. The agent has to inspect the code, form a hypothesis, make a change, run tests, and revise its approach if it fails. The difficulty is maintaining progress through that loop.

Further along, you have open-ended tasks like doing research. Now even the definition of success may be unclear. The agent has to decide which questions to pursue, what evidence is sufficient, and when to stop. That requires judgment as well as execution.

So I wouldn’t classify difficulty just by the number of tool calls. A long task with clear feedback can be easier than a short task with an ambiguous objective. The key question is how much uncertainty the agent has to resolve on its own, and whether the environment gives it useful feedback along the way.

r001.rationale: The response identifies task definition, duration, and ease of verification as distinct dimensions, saying they are related but not the same.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare task difficulty for humans with task difficulty for AI agents.
